content.text: Why does a person wearing stiletto heels sink into soft ground, while the same person wearing flat shoes does not? Why can a sharp knife cut through food easily, while a blunt knife struggles? The answer lies in the concept of
— the force acting per unit area.

Pressure is a concept that appears throughout physics, from the behaviour of gases to the design of hydraulic systems, from weather forecasting to deep-sea exploration. In this lesson, we will define pressure, explore how it applies to solids, liquids, and the atmosphere, and learn about hydraulic systems and their practical applications.

One pascal is a very small pressure. Common pressures are often expressed in kilopascals (kPa) or megapascals (MPa):
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 101 kPa (about 100 kPa for rough calculations).
For a given force, the pressure depends on the area:
A drawing pin: The sharp point has a very small area, so even a small force produces a very large pressure, allowing it to pierce the material.
Snowshoes: Large surface area spreads the person's weight over a bigger area, reducing the pressure on the snow and preventing the person from sinking.
A knife: A sharp blade has a very small contact area at its edge, creating high pressure that can cut through materials.
A camel's wide feet: Spread the camel's weight over a large area, reducing pressure on the sand.
Tractor tyres: Wide tyres spread the weight of the tractor, reducing pressure on soft soil.
Liquids exert pressure on any surface in contact with them. This pressure has important characteristics:
The deeper you go, the more liquid is above you, and the greater the weight of liquid pushing down.
at a given point in a liquid. Unlike pressure in a solid (which acts in one direction — perpendicular to the surfaces in contact), liquid pressure pushes equally in every direction.
Pressure at a given depth is the same in all directions.
Pressure does not depend on the shape of the container
— only on the depth and the density of the liquid.

pressure is transmitted equally throughout a confined liquid
(Pascal's principle). This allows a small force on a small piston to create a large force on a large piston.
When pressure is applied to an enclosed fluid, the pressure is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container.

"Pressure and force are the same thing."
Pressure is force per unit area. A small force can create a large pressure (if the area is small), and a large force can create a small pressure (if the area is large).
"Pressure in a liquid acts only downward."
at any given point. A hole in the side of a container will spray water outward (not downward) with a force related to the depth.
"A wider container has more pressure at the bottom."

Pressure at a given depth depends only on the density of the liquid, gravitational field strength, and depth — not on the shape or width of the container. This is sometimes called the "hydrostatic paradox."
Hydraulic systems do not create energy. They multiply force at the expense of distance. The work done is the same on both sides (minus any friction losses).
Atmospheric pressure acts in all directions — upward, downward, and sideways.
"We feel the pressure of the atmosphere pushing on us."

We do not normally feel atmospheric pressure because it pushes equally on all sides and is balanced by the pressure inside our bodies. We only notice changes in pressure (e.g., in an aeroplane or going up a mountain).
The density of water is essentially the same at all depths (water is nearly incompressible). The pressure increases because there is more water above pushing down.

Dams are thicker at the base because water pressure increases with depth ($P = \rho gh$). At the bottom of a 40 m deep dam: $P = 1000 \times 10 \times 40 = 400\,000$ Pa. At 10 m depth: $P = 100\,000$ Pa. The base must withstand 4 times the pressure of a point 10 m deep, so it needs to be much thicker to resist this greater force.
